title: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: v(\theta + n) = x^n v(\theta) for a rise of n degrees; temperature coefficient of growth x^{10} \approx 2\text{--}3

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Van’t Hoff’s law, which has become a fundamental principle of chemical mechanics, is likewise applicable (with certain qualifications) to the phenomena of vital chemistry; and it follows that, on very much the same lines, we may speak of the “temperature coefficient” of growth.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Effect of temperature”. Scope: growth and development of plants and animals within normal temperature limits

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: v(\theta + n) = x^n v(\theta) for a rise of n degrees; temperature coefficient of growth x^{10} \approx 2\text{--}3

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-21: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mathematical response and coefficient are explicit and widely measured, and open experimental data can support tests across representative plants and animals. Broad synthesis requires harmonization, but standard regressions can resolve the qualified claim with current data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit growth or development rates across temperatures within normal ranges and calculate Q10 values, testing whether rates rise approximately exponentially and Q10 commonly lies between two and three. Systematic non-exponential responses or Q10 values outside that range would refute the stated law.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Q10 varies with temperature interval and proximity to thermal limits.

Relevant experiments require compilation from many deposits.

Field time series confound temperature with season.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.95
discriminating power: 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A Q10 between about 2 and 3 is a numerical criterion, and both raw rates and fitted temperature coefficients exist for many species. They are not one openly complete table for plants and animals inside normal limits, and the coefficient's dependence on the chosen interval is a built-in ambiguity the claim already flags. A compiled subset can test the order of magnitude; it does not cover the full scope in a single standard analysis.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Below the optimum, compute the factor by which growth rate changes per 10°C. A factor of about 2 to 3, the same order as ordinary chemical reactions, would support the claim. A factor near 1 across the normal range, or systematically an order of magnitude larger, would refute the stated similarity. Intervals above the optimum are outside the qualified claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Fitted temperature parameters are not the same object as a raw rate ratio, and tabulated Q10 values are a sparse sample.

The coefficient itself falls as the temperature interval rises, so the test range has to be declared.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.65
data existence: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.45
